item.title: ‘We’re recording you too, bud:’ body-worn cameras, citizen journalism, and the changing landscape of police visibility
item.description:
Authors: Ajay Sandhu & Sara K. Thompson
Journal: Policing & Society

The widespread adoption of body-worn cameras (BWCs) has transformed the landscape of police visibility. While BWCs are commonly understood as technologies for evidence collection and police accountability, less attention has been paid to how police officers themselves understand the technology as a means of responding to citizen journalism. item.description:
Authors: David McDowall et al.
Journal: Injury Prevention

BACKGROUND: Injury-provoking violence is an important concern among police officers, and it influences their decisions about using force in their encounters with civilians. We sought to estimate the occurrence and trends in non-fatal assaults on police officers in the USA. METHODS: We estimated rates and frequencies of assaults directed against working police officers during four periods: 1993-1999, 2000-2005, 2007-2015 and 2016-2021. Authors: Félicien Faury et al.
Journal: Policing & Society

However, this process of visibilisation is not an automatic one. This article posits that an understanding of the phenomenon of policing's new visibility should integrate the role of intermediaries between ordinary people filming the police and the large-scale publicisation of images of police brutality. item.description:
Authors: Julia Rodríguez Pantel
Journal: Critical Criminology

Abstract This article examines police violence through a spatial lens. It performs a micro-sociological qualitative analysis of body-worn camera (BWC) video data of 17 cases of police operations. Methodologically, the study combines grounded theory and systematic video data analysis (VDA). The hypothesis-generating study examines interactions between officers and civilians, along with their situational outcomes, within the context of spatial contestations of the public and the private. item.description:
Authors: Benjamin Carleton & Thomas Christoff
Journal: Policing An International Journal

Purpose Early intervention (EI) systems have been implemented in law enforcement agencies across the country as a tool for improving accountability, officer wellness, and overall data management. While the term “early intervention system” is commonly used within law enforcement, approaches and processes vary widely across agencies. This omission is important because of overlapping risk factors and potential compounding harm.
